items.title: Trump's Push To Reinstate Huang, Market Reacts To Nvidia, Russia-Ukraine War Widening
items.summary: President Trump says he pushed Nvidia to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO, raising questions about why the White House is getting involved in who runs a private company. Nvidia gained nearly a trillion dollars in value after Huang returned, showing how much of the A-I economy is tied to one company and one man. Russia’s war in Ukraine is spreading far beyond the battlefield, even as the Trump administration says talks toward a peace deal are making progress.

items.title: Wild turkeys are in peril again — can researchers save them?
items.summary: As a teen, Mike Chamberlain spent all his free time hunting turkeys. Now, his job is researching everything about them – the birds’ behavior, their genetics and more. And for the past decade, he’s focused on their concerning decline in the American southeast. Today on the show, Emily chats with Mike about what could be driving the loss of turkey territory – and what conservationists – including hunters – are doing about it. Interested in more conservation science? Email us your question at shortwave@npr.org .

items.title: Trump faces backlash after saying he 'convinced' Nvidia to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang
items.summary: Nvidia had come under pressure from President Trump to reappoint Huang, whose comeback helped add $1tn to the company's stock value.
items.body: Jensen Huang has been reinstated as the boss of Nvidia less than two weeks after he was forced to resign following the revelations of extra marital affairs, one of which was with a suspected Chinese spy. The AI chipmaker handed its co-founder his job back, despite rejecting his initial offer to return, after pressure from US President Donald Trump.

items.title: Car bomb tears through Colombian city wounding more than 20
items.summary: The explosion is the latest in a string of attacks on buildings housing the security forces and government offices.
items.body: A car bomb has exploded in the central Colombian city of Villavicencio, injuring at least 23 people. The explosive device was detonated in front of the offices of the regional government, in the city centre, damaging several buildings.

items.title: DR Congo says military aircraft missing as rebels claim to shoot down plane
items.summary: A South African fighter pilot and a Ugandan officer are reportedly among those aboard the downed plane.
items.body: The Democratic Republic of Congo military says it is searching for one of its aircraft, after rebels said they had shot down a warplane in the east. The military said it had lost contact with a small Cessna 208 cargo plane on Sunday following "poor weather conditions". The fate of the plane and its crew remained uncertain, it added.

items.title: Ukraine confirms it used naval drones to strike two Russian ships off Libya
items.summary: Ukraine’s security service says seven drones were launched from mothership in operation that sank Merkury warship Ukraine has confirmed it deployed naval drones in strikes on two Russian vessels off Libya on Sunday, including one that sank the corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest vessels. Ukraine’s security service, the SBU, said seven domestically made naval drones were launched from a mothership in the operation, which Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as “exemplary”.

items.title: Robert Pattinson is not enough: who should become the new Bond girl?
items.summary: With the British actor securing the role of James Bond, speculation has now begun over who should join him in Denis Villeneuve’s much-anticipated caper After years of speculation, Robert Pattinson has been officially cast as James Bond for a new Amazon-produced film directed by Denis Villeneuve. There’s no release date for the project yet, though fall 2028 seems a likely target, given the release dates of all of the Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig installments. This leaves plenty of time left on the clock for more speculation – namely, about who will be cast as the so-called Bond Girls for this rebooted installment. Past Bonds have usually been recognizable from earlier work, but none of them had yet reached Pattinson’s level of fame before actually playing Bond. Given that, in addition to sterling indie work for directors like David Cronenberg, Claire Denis and Lance Oppenheim, Pattinson has also been in Twilight, Batman and Christopher Nolan movies, he’s arguably already as famous as Brosnan and Craig were at their 007 peak. It must be this shift in the casting status quo that has inspired some predictions or hopes for a quantity as known as, say, Sydney Sweeney to play a Bond girl.
items.body: After years of speculation, Robert Pattinson has been officially cast as James Bond for a new Amazon-produced film directed by Denis Villeneuve. There’s no release date for the project yet, though fall 2028 seems a likely target, given the release dates of all of the Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig installments.

items.title: Man Theft Auto – why did so few women review GTA VI, the biggest video game of the decade?
items.summary: Given that this is the first Grand Theft Auto in 30 years with a female protagonist, you might have expected to hear from female critics. But you would have expected mostly in vain Grand Theft Auto VI is now the biggest video game launch of all time, and is likely to become the biggest video game of all time. It’s a once-in-a-lifetime event, a phenomenon that will shape games as a medium and pop culture at large for years to come, set against the backdrop of its developers fighting for their rights at studio Rockstar Games . It has snatched sales and streaming records and become the best-reviewed game ever (pulling ahead of 1998’s The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time). It’s also the first GTA game with a female protagonist, who also happens to be a woman of colour. Yet very few women (and seemingly no women of colour) played and reviewed it before release. When GTA IV’s review embargo lifted on 18 November, the gender imbalance was immediately obvious. Out of 156 reviewers, only six appeared to be women. As journalist Lex Luddy noted in a BlueSky post , that is 3.8%.
items.body: Grand Theft Auto VI is now the biggest video game launch of all time, and is likely to become the biggest video game of all time.

items.title: From Sovereigns to Servants by Alexandra Prokopenko review – Putin and his yes men
items.summary: A disturbing account of the way Russia’s elites have reduced themselves to craven courtiers When Vladimir Putin launched his full-scale invasion of Ukraine four and a half years ago, it was a shock, but it wasn’t a surprise. The US and the UK had been publicly warning their allies for weeks about what Russia was planning, as well as threatening the Russians with a wave of sanctions unprecedented against a major power. Putin’s foreign policy had long relied on confusion and untruth. By saying that they knew exactly what he was up to, Britain and America were hoping first to deny him his usual ambiguity, and second to pressure the men around him into making him stop, since war would deprive them of the stolen assets they’d stashed in London’s most exclusive neighbourhoods.

items.title: Cop31 failed. What happens now? – podcast
items.summary: The longest ever Cop climate talks have ended in failure after countries were unable to agree a deal. The key sticking point was the omission of any mention of fossil fuels in the final draft. items.title: Why we’re still thinking about the Roman empire
items.summary: Why does Rome loom so large in the popular mindset – arguably more so than any other ancient civilisation – and what can that reveal about how we understand the past? Emily Briffett speaks with historian Rhiannon Garth Jones about her book All Roads Lead to Rome, to explore how the idea of Rome has been endlessly reused, reshaped and repurposed from ancient empire to modern politics and pop culture. Together, they consider the question: does Rome still matter today? ----- GO BEYOND THE PODCAST Curious to find out more about the Abbasid caliphate mentioned in the episode? items.title: On this day: 24 November
items.summary: 2023 — Hibiscus Rising, commemorating David Oluwale, is unveiled in Leeds.
items.body:
2023 — Hibiscus Rising, commemorating David Oluwale, is unveiled in Leeds.

2022 — Five days after the general elections which resulted in a hung parliament, opposition leader and former deputy prime minister Anwar Ibrahim is officially named as the 10th prime minister of Malaysia.

2017 — A terrorist attack on a Mosque in Al-Rawda, North Sinai, Egypt kills 311 people and injures 128.

2016 — The government of Colombia and the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia–People's Army sign a revised peace deal, bringing an end to the country's more than 50-year-long civil war.

2015 — A Russian Air Force Sukhoi Su-24 fighter jet is shot down by the Turkish Air Force over the Syria–Turkey border, killing one of the two pilots; a Russian marine is also killed during a subsequent rescue effort.
